run `kimi` in the terminal to start; on first use, log in to the Kimi Code platform with the `/login` command to complete the connection — no need to manually manage an API Key.

supports `low` / `high` / `max` thinking effort levels. Best for large codebase analysis, multi-file refactoring, and long-document processing.

K3 API pricing of $3/$15 per 1M tokens is called extremely high for a Chinese open-weight model, matching Sonnet. The commenter warns heavy reasoning-token use could make it costlier in practice than reasoning-efficient GPT models.
One user observed that K3 seems to use only about 60% as many reasoning tokens as K2.6, so the price hike is not as bad as it looks.
A user found that K3 seems to have kept the K2 series' creative writing abilities, at least with the prompts they had tested so far.
Complaint: account creation is only possible with a phone number or a Google account, which the user called lame.
"Not worth it. I have just tried a single prompt in the web interface and it is still not finish reasoning. It thinks too much and often repeats the same stuff over and over."
A user with a free GitHub Copilot quota says Kimi K2.7 is the model they are most happy with among those available, given its cost/performance.

K3 API parameters are inflexible: reasoning_effort supports only "max" with thinking always on, temperature/top_p are fixed, vision input doesn't accept public image URLs, and web search isn't recommended for production.

On a Tiananmen Square test via kimi.com, K2 without Thinking refused: "I can't provide information on this topic." With Thinking on, it pulled from Wikipedia and described the 1989 protests and estimated death tolls.
"The non-thinking version is the best writer by far." The user says Moonshot "really cooked" something different from other frontier labs.
K2 Thinking was the only recent model that gave a human-like solution to the egg/object stacking problem on the first try.
Praise for K3 versus Fable: "A third the cost, open source, and won't refuse every other request because of some vague possible connection to cybersecurity concerns."
A DeepSeek user says Kimi K3 now offers a great planning assistant for more advanced coding tasks (Rust, PSQL, Angular, Terraform).
In FastAPI/Spring Boot tasks, GLM-5.2 and Kimi spend roughly 70–80K tokens grepping the codebase before writing anything, then typically break the code. The user says Qwen3.7-Max "just… does it."
Skeptic citing arena.ai: Fable 5 dominates almost every category, while Kimi K3 has an edge in WebDev but struggles to reach the top 10 in many others.
Trialing K2.6 through a work subscription: "so far it looks on par, if not better, than opus."
"I've always been surprised Kimi doesn't get more attention than it does. It's always stood out to me in terms of creativity, quality... has been my favorite model for awhile."
Kimi 2.5 was really good for design but borderline useless on backend/advanced tasks; using OpenCode instead of the Kimi CLI really hurt performance.
Running K2.6 through OpenCode to Kimi's API, it "overthinks": pages of thought, 50k+ output tokens going in circles without doing anything — complete analysis paralysis.

In one user's tests, K2.6 did only slightly better than K2.5, struggling with puzzle and trick-style exactness tasks with frequent instruction misses. Probably a great coding model, but less intelligent overall than SOTA.
K2.6 couldn't solve the user's mixed-up wolf/goat/cabbage puzzle. Sonnet 4.6 also failed, while Opus 4.7 had no problems.

PROBE runtime (recorded 2026-10-01): kimi.com publishes NO llms.txt — https://www.kimi.com/llms.txt answers HTTP 302 Location: / (the SPA root) instead of an agent docs index, and the assistant app has no docs site at all. The real llms.txt at platform.kimi.ai/docs/llms.txt belongs to the Kimi API Open Platform, which the vendor's own product-plans doc distinguishes as a separate pay-as-you-go product from the Kimi assistant/Membership. kimi.com also serves its landing content in Chinese to our fetcher, and the membership pricing page (www.kimi.ai/membership/pricing) renders client-side only — no tier prices reach a keyless fetch.

PROBE runtime (recorded 2026-10-01): the vendor's product-plans doc (fetched keylessly as markdown) states 'Kimi Membership currently includes Kimi Code benefits' across its four membership subscription tiers, and the official Kimi Code docs at https://www.kimi.com/code/docs/en/ serve keylessly ('Kimi Code' verified in the page) — an official CLI bundled with the consumer subscription. No public API for the assistant app itself: the Kimi API on platform.kimi.ai is the separate Open Platform product per the same doc.

The Kimi API Platform (platform.kimi.ai, the international developer platform for Moonshot AI's Kimi) publishes a downloadable OpenAPI 3.1.0 document ("Moonshot AI API", "API for Moonshot AI / Kimi large language model services", server https://api.moonshot.ai; /v1 chat completions, responses, Anthropic-compatible messages, batches, files, tool search, and models), referenced from the docs pages, plus a separate dated Admin API spec (row kimi-admin-openapi-20261106). Both download unauthenticated.

"The Kimi Admin API lets organization administrators manage members, invitations, projects, and inference API keys programmatically, and query billing, usage, and audit logs" - a second OpenAPI document (3.0.3) carrying a date-based version (2026-10-20-beta).

The Mintlify-hosted API reference runs the "Try it" playground per endpoint (docs and runner load without login; executing needs an API key against the production endpoint). A separate login-gated console playground exists ("Compare models, tune parameters, test tool calls, and turn successful experiments into API requests with Kimi Playground.").

The API is /v1 path-versioned (OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible bases) and the platform publishes a dated model deprecation table with migration guidance covering API model IDs ("## Deprecated Models"; e.g. "No longer available to newly registered users; users registered before November 1 can continue using it. Deprecation expected in late December 2026."), and the Admin API spec itself is date-versioned. Caveats: no API changelog page and no standalone deprecation-policy document (the platform docs host also soft-200s unknown paths, so these absences are grounded in the full llms.txt index).

"The Kimi intelligent assistant can upload files and answer questions based on those files. The Kimi API offers the same functionality." The guide walks through uploading files, extracting their contents, and adding them to conversations for single-file or multi-file question answering, and the files API uploads "for text content extraction, image understanding, or video understanding" (pdf, doc, txt and more).

Kimi documents key isolation and restriction at the project level: "You can create multiple projects in an organization and multiple API keys in each project", with the console used to "set project budgets and rate limits, manage members, configure an IP whitelist, and review organization and project consumption"; "API usage is tracked separately for each project, so you can monitor and manage spending by project", and each member creates their own key per project. Scope caveat: restrictions attach to projects (budgets, rate limits, IP whitelist, membership), not per-key permission scopes.

Scope of the kimi.com assistant surface: kimi.com serves its client-rendered app shell for every path including llms.txt (soft-200; the body is the JS application with a release-version meta tag, no agent-oriented docs file). The real llms.txt at platform.kimi.ai/docs/llms.txt belongs to the separate Kimi API Open Platform. The only assistant capability the citable vendor text documents is file upload with question answering ("The Kimi intelligent assistant can upload files and answer questions based on those files."); image and video understanding are documented for the API surface (the files API and the vision-model guide), not for the assistant app.
